summary: Describes how Mobile IPv6 Fast Handovers could be implemented on 802.11 wireless links. Fast handovers aim to reduce the interruption when a mobile device moves from one access point's network to another. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Walking between Wi-Fi spots can cut your connection for a moment. This memo shows how to hand your connection over to the next spot smoothly.

subtitle: Keeping WiFi connections alive during handoffs between access points.

tldr.problem: Mobile devices lose their internet connection briefly when roaming between WiFi access points. This interruption is unacceptable for real-time services like voice calls.
tldr.mechanism: Mobile IPv6 Fast Handover (FMIPv6) uses information from 802.11 link-layer handover events to set up a tunnel between the old and new access routers. This allows the device to maintain IP connectivity before fully registering with the new network.
tldr.outcome: This document shows how FMIPv6 could work on 802.11 networks by describing the timing of handover events and message exchanges. It remains informational guidance for implementers.

today: RFC 4260 remains informational guidance for implementing FMIPv6 on 802.11 networks. It has not been obsoleted or updated. The underlying FMIPv6 specification (RFC 4068) was itself made Historic by RFC 6275, so the techniques described are no longer recommended for new deployments.

sections.title: The Problem and the Solution
sections.content:
Mobile IPv6 provides a way for devices to maintain connectivity as they move between networks. However, without fast handover mechanisms, devices face a gap in service: the time between disconnecting from one access point and registering with a new one. This gap can be hundreds of milliseconds, which disrupts real-time services like voice calls.

Fast Handover works by leveraging information from the wireless link layer. When a device begins to lose signal to one access point, it can initiate communication with the new access point's router before completing the full handover. By establishing a tunnel between the old and new access routers, the device can receive traffic destined for it even before it finishes registering its new address. This approach reduces the service interruption dramatically.
sections.eli5: Before your phone loses one WiFi signal, it tells the old router about the new one it is connecting to. The old router keeps forwarding your data to the new one, so you do not lose connection.

sections.title: How 802.11 Handovers Work
sections.content:
An 802.11 handover (roaming) happens in several steps. First, the device scans for nearby access points and measures signal strength. This scan can take 100 to 300 milliseconds, during which the device cannot send or receive traffic. The device then synchronizes with the target access point, authenticates with it, and associates. During this process, layer-2 (MAC address) information is updated, and security procedures may be performed using 802.1X or 802.11i.

Importantly, changing access points does not automatically mean the device moves to a new IP subnet. In some deployments, multiple access points serve the same subnet. In others, each access point is connected to a different subnet. This difference is critical for understanding when IP-layer mobility mechanisms are needed.
sections.eli5: Your phone searches for WiFi signals, picks the best one, talks to it in WiFi language, and asks permission to join. All of this takes time.

sections.title: Fast Handover Message Exchange
sections.content:
FMIPv6 defines a sequence of messages exchanged during a handover. The mobile node first sends a Router Solicitation for Proxy (RtSolPr) to learn about neighboring access routers. It receives back a Proxy Router Advertisement (PrRtAdv) containing information about available routers. The node then sends a Fast Binding Update (FBU) to its current router, which initiates a Handover Initiate (HI) message to the new router. The new router acknowledges with Handover Acknowledge (HAck), and the old router forwards a Fast Binding Acknowledgement (FBack) to the new link.

The critical insight is that these FMIPv6 messages can be exchanged at different times relative to the 802.11 handover. A predictive approach sends FBU before the handover is complete. A reactive approach completes the handover first, then sends the FBU from the new network. This flexibility allows implementations to adapt to hardware capabilities and radio conditions.
sections.eli5: The phone and routers exchange a few messages: the phone asks about the new router, tells the old router it is leaving, the old router warns the new router, and then the new router welcomes the phone.

sections.title: Deployment Architectures
sections.content:
The document describes two main deployment models. In the first, relay access points serve as layer-2 bridges connecting to a distribution system. Multiple access points can serve the same IP subnet, so a device moving between them stays on the same subnet and may not need IP-level mobility at all. In the second model, each access point is integrated directly with an access router on a separate subnet. Here, every access point change requires an IP-layer handover.

Understanding the deployment architecture is essential for FMIPv6 implementation. In the relay model, a device can determine whether IP-layer handover is needed by checking if the new access point reaches the same subnet. In the integrated model, the device knows that every handover requires IP mobility management. The MAC-layer address of the access point may directly indicate the access router's identity in integrated deployments.
sections.eli5: There are two ways to set up WiFi: many routers sharing one internet connection, or each router having its own connection. FMIPv6 works differently in each case.

sections.title: Implementation Scenarios
sections.content:
The RFC presents three scenarios for how 802.11 and FMIPv6 events can interleave. Scenario 1 (predictive mode) is optimal: the device scans for access points and sends a Fast Binding Update to the old router before the 802.11 handover completes. Only a Fast Neighbor Advertisement is sent after handover. This requires that the device driver can control scan and join operations independently.

Scenario 2 (reactive with advance knowledge) has the device obtain the new router's link-layer address before handover, but completes the 802.11 handover before sending the FBU. Scenario 3 (fully reactive) performs no advance discovery; the device completes the handover first, then discovers the new router and sends the binding update. The choice of scenario depends on hardware capabilities, radio conditions, and the network deployment model. Implementations may fall back from predictive to reactive modes if radio conditions change unexpectedly.
sections.eli5: Three ways work: learning about the new router before handover and staying ahead of it, discovering it as you switch, or learning about it after you arrive.

sections.title: Security
sections.content:
The security properties of FMIPv6 depend on the underlying 802.11 security mechanisms and the authentication used for the Fast Binding Update. The previous access router must verify that the FBU genuinely comes from the mobile node before redirecting traffic. However, if the association with the new access point is not protected by mutual authentication, a rogue access point could trick the mobile node into sending an FBU.

The RFC notes that Wired Equivalent Privacy (WEP) shared key authentication is weak and should not be relied upon. Instead, the Robust Security Network (RSN) uses 802.1X and EAP for authentication. The 802.1X pre-authentication feature allows a device to authenticate with the new access point while still associated with the old one, enabling faster service resumption. However, pre-authentication currently works only within a single VLAN and does not help for cross-subnet handovers where FMIPv6 is most needed. Cross-subnet authentication with FMIPv6 remains an area for future work.
sections.eli5: The system needs to make sure it is talking to the real new router, not a fake one. Modern WiFi security (802.1X) can help, but it adds more waiting time.
